doc.title: Earl Watkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

chapter: Big bands in the Bay Area
title: Sonny Greer and Hampton's drummers
summary: Front row at the auditorium, he admires Sonny Greer and repeats Ernie Royal's story of Greer sitting in with Hampton.

bands.name: Louis Jordan and His Tympany Five

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: So would you be one — would you be on the dance floor or would you be one of those fellas that was like up —

Front row. Oh yeah. I was married at the time. My ex-wife, ooh, she used to get uptight. She’d get so mad because she loved to dance. I’d be either up front of else in the wings where I could watch the drummers. And Sonny Greer, now, was the most underrated drummer. He never got any publicity. But he held that band together. He was a burner, I mean for drums. In later years, when you look for something else, and if you listen to the records, you’ll find he’s another fella that fit that Duke band like a glove. Like there was one tune called “Cotton Tail,” which is a classic with Ben Webster. You know he made it really. But if you listen to the drums back there, and how he’s kicking. And then when the band goes [scats] you just listen to what he’s doing behind the band. And Ernie Royal, we were talking about Duke’s band one time and talking about the drummers, because they used to talk about Hamp’s band, see as I said before Marshall and Ernie and Vernon and Irvin Ashby, they were all in the first — Hamp’s band, the first Lionel Hampton band that made “Flying Home.” And Ernie said that they always had trouble with drummers. Because Lionel was a drummer, and he’d want them to play that heavy bass drum, and they’d wear out drummers. So he said, Sonny — one time Sonny Greer came in and they had to play a show and their drummer wasn’t available. And Sonny Greer came in and he played the show so great and kicked that band so great that the owner of the nightclub wanted to hire him on the spot. Well naturally he couldn’t because he was Duke’s drummer.
Yeah you don’t raid Duke’s band, do you?

Oh man, no, no, man. But anyhow with that auditorium during the war, you have everybody that came through there. I saw Louis Jordan with his Tympani Five. Oh who the heck else? Well I named off quite a few, who’s left?
